title: Following a Claim Back to Its Source

callouts.label: Footnote 4 of the resource
callouts.hint: A page with a small footnote mark at the bottom, inside a speech bubble.
callouts.description: The claim "Wetlands filter pollutants" appears in the resource. Footnote 4 cites a textbook. This link is someone's summary and is not the original.
callouts.tip: A footnote tells you where to look next. It is not evidence by itself.

callouts.label: The textbook
callouts.hint: A closed book with a red stop sign on a flag pole.
callouts.description: The textbook says wetlands filter pollutants and cites a review. A reviewer who stops here, at the red flag, has found only that a textbook agrees with the resource.
callouts.tip: This is the early stop the poster exists to prevent.

callouts.label: The review article
callouts.hint: Stacked pages in two columns, inside a speech bubble.
callouts.description: The review article summarizes several studies of wetland filtering. It is another summary, so it is not the original either.
callouts.tip: Secondary sources describe, summarize, or interpret primary sources.

callouts.label: The original study
callouts.hint: A laboratory bench with a flask and a gauge inside a six-sided shape, the only link not in a speech bubble.
callouts.description: One of those studies reports measurements of pollutant levels before and after water passed through a wetland. This is the original, and the claim is supported by it.
callouts.tip: The further back you trace a claim, the more you can trust the check. The sources in this example are invented.
